tool.name: London dichroscope
tool.measures: pleochroism: the different colours of a coloured stone depending on the direction of observation (two halves, A and B)
tool.where: Gemmology House and Office, top row, in the middle of the laboratory (a lamp is placed underneath)
tips: Turn the stone in all directions, through a full turn
Compare the two windows A and B
It also works on a set stone, without touching it

steps.title: Pleochroism
steps.text: Some coloured stones do not have the same colour when seen from different directions: this is pleochroism. Light goes through the crystal differently depending on the axis, and each direction absorbs other colours. A ruby, seen one way, looks red; seen another way, it looks orange-red.

steps.title: The London dichroscope
steps.text: With the naked eye, the two colours of a pleochroic stone mix and you only see an average shade. The London dichroscope separates them. It is a small folding loupe that contains two polarizing filters glued at right angles, each in one half of the lens. Each filter only lets through a single direction of vibration of the light: half A shows one of the two colours of the stone, half B the other. You look at the stone through both halves at once, and compare.

steps.title: None, two or three colours
Using the dichroscope
steps.text: 1. Put the stone on a well-lit surface: the lamp of the laboratory. 2. Bring the London dichroscope close to your eye and look at the stone through the lens: it appears in both halves, A and B. 3. Turn the stone a full turn, then in other directions: pleochroism only shows in certain positions. 4. If A and B differ at some point, the stone is pleochroic; if they stay the same everywhere, it is not. You need a coloured, transparent stone: a very pale or colourless stone gives little result.

steps.title: The London dichroscope and the calcite dichroscope
steps.text: The London dichroscope is the one of the laboratory, and the one you use here: two polarizing filters glued perpendicular to each other in a folding loupe, simple, light, fits in a pocket. There is another model, the calcite dichroscope: a crystal of Iceland spar splits the light into two beams and gives two images side by side. You find it at the GemStore, for the bag. Both rely on the same idea: separating the two directions of vibration of light. Neither one touches the stone: they even work on a set stone, in a piece of jewellery.

steps.title: A few examples
steps.text: • Ruby: red / orange-red. • Blue sapphire: blue / blue-green. • Emerald: blue-green / yellow-green. • Tanzanite: blue / violet / red-brown. • Iolite: blue / violet / pale yellow. • Spinel: no change. A red spinel therefore cannot pass for a ruby in front of a dichroscope: it is one of the finest tests of gemmology.
